log.rationale: Eleven of the eighteen failures are AgentTimeoutError with zero recorded steps and cost: the run wedged on a long or interactive foreground command (a build, a training run, an emulator, a download) and never came back to the model. The fix is a concrete procedure for long work rather than a policy: give every command an explicit time limit, push anything that can outlast a couple of minutes into a background job and poll it, and starve interactive prompts of stdin so nothing waits on a keypress. This keeps the loop turning on exactly the compile/train/emulate tasks that timed out, and costs nothing on the short tasks that already pass.

Timeouts still dominate the losses and several arrive with 'steps None, $0.00' — meaning the very first foreground command wedged and the whole hour was spent blocked before any step was recorded (crack-7z-hash and make-mips-interpreter time out on one run but pass the other at a few cents, gcode-to-text wedges on both runs of a trivial task). The i1 edit told the model to background long work but left the foreground time limit as a soft example ('e.g. 2m'), so the model can still pass a huge or open-ended limit on a command that then eats the session. The fix makes the cap a hard, concrete rule: the second argument is mandatory and must never exceed 2 minutes for a foreground call, and anything that could plausibly outlast that goes to the background even when you are unsure — an unknown-duration command is treated as long by default. This keeps the loop turning on the compile/crack/emulate tasks that intermittently wedge, and costs nothing on short tasks that already finish well under the cap.

Two of the standing losses end 'claimed' with real steps and no timeout, yet fail the most basic tests: sam-cell-seg fails test_run_script and test_csv_output_exists (the deliverable never actually produced its output file), and the failing path-tracing run fails test_image_compiles and test_runs_and_produces_output (claimed done without compiling or running). The model edits source and reasons about correctness but stops before executing the deliverable end-to-end on the real input, so a script that crashes or emits nothing, or a program that never compiles, is reported as finished. The fix is a concrete final-verification procedure: run the exact deliverable the brief names to completion, confirm the output artifact exists, and inspect its structure (types, shapes, row/column counts, that lists are flat not nested) against the brief before claiming. This attacks the 'claimed but never ran' pattern generally without pressuring the timeout-bound tasks, so it should flip sam-cell-seg and the failing path-tracing run while risking nothing that already passes.

The remaining losses are dominated by AgentTimeoutError with 'steps None, $0.00' — the very first foreground command wedged and the whole hour drained before a single step was recorded. gcode-to-text is the tell: a trivial task (write a hello file) that times out on BOTH runs at zero cost, which only happens when first contact drops into a pager or an interpreter/REPL that blocks on stdin so the poll never returns. i2's blunt 2m cap over-corrected and regressed passing tasks, so this edit is narrow: extend the existing interactive-programs rule to also kill pagers and never launch an interpreter/debugger/unknown binary without feeding it `< /dev/null`, plus a recovery step (a command that returns nothing while still alive is waiting on input — kill and rerun non-interactively). This turns the loop over on step one without pressuring the genuinely long compile/train tasks.

The one reproducible non-timeout loss is sam-cell-seg (0/2, real steps, ends 'claimed'): it fails test_run_script and test_csv_output_exists, meaning the model edited source and reasoned about correctness but never executed the named deliverable to completion, so a script that crashes or emits nothing was reported as done. The failing path-tracing run shows the same shape (claimed without compiling/running). The fix is one concrete final step, not a policy: run the exact command the brief names once on the real input, then confirm the output artifact exists and is non-empty before claiming; a crash or empty output means not done. I keep this to a single tight sentence appended to the existing brief to avoid the dilution that sank the verbose i3 attempt, and it does not pressure the genuinely long compile/train tasks.
